A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SPACE and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained content can be matched across the substantial changes in layout and experimental coverage.

before.justification: v1 reports original corruption-benchmark experiments, local/global feature analyses, and supplementary kernel-embedding and DVS Gesture-C results.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark experiments, including ImageNet and ConvLSTM evaluations, together with alignment-objective and augmentation-count ablations.

M1.justification: Standard SPACE retains its spike-count representation, channel-wise consistency objective, and single adaptation step. Appendix B introduces two implemented experimental variants that instead align temporally averaged membrane potentials or time-resolved spikes. These are auxiliary procedure additions, not replacements for standard SPACE.

E1.justification: v2 adds ImageNet-V2, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, extending evaluation to recollected images, artistic renditions, and naturally challenging images. CIFAR coverage changes from 18/19 corruptions to 15: four corruption types are removed, and glass blur is added for CIFAR-10-C. DVS Gesture-C and its six corruption types were already evaluated in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: The corresponding benchmark comparisons retain MEMO, SITA where applicable, and the unadapted control, renamed from w.o. TTA to No Adapt. Appendix B/Table 5 adds comparisons against two SPACE objective variants, using average membrane potentials and time-resolved spikes. No new external TTA baseline is introduced.

E3.justification: DVS evaluation replaces the 2CONV-2FC backbone with a 2ConvLSTM-1FC model. New ImageNet experiments use a 19M-parameter Spike-driven Transformer V3 and 64 augmentations. Appendix C introduces an augmentation-count sweep from 2 to 128 and per-input runtime measurement. The retained CNN experiments preserve their stated inference-step counts and single adaptation update.

E4.justification: New appendices B and C test the choice of alignment representation and the accuracy/runtime consequences of augmentation quantity. The existing kernel and local/global analyses remain, with revised corruption coverage. The Gaussian Blur similarity-distribution analysis from v1 Figure 4 is removed; v2 Figure 3b retains only Impulse Noise.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, accuracy error bars, or significance tests. The feature-similarity histograms describe feature distributions rather than uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds ImageNet results, including SPACE's 43.37% average, and objective/runtime ablation results. It replaces the old DVS backbone's results, including 57.14% for SPACE, with ConvLSTM results reporting 65.91%; these are different settings. CIFAR aggregates change with corruption coverage. Within retained CIFAR-10-C/VGG9 comparisons, MEMO's JPEG score changes from 86.05% to 85.05% and elastic-transform accuracy from 76.24% to 76.45%. Tiny-ImageNet-C scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The LIF and surrogate-gradient expressions, standard SPACE similarity/loss, and kernel/MMD derivation are retained. v2 consolidates alignment equations and expresses the gradient update in prose. These changes do not introduce a substantive mathematical correction, assumption, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions explicitly extend architectural generality from VGG/ResNet to CNN, Transformer, and ConvLSTM families and include ImageNet benchmarks. The central novelty claim of source-free, single-instance TTA tailored to SNNs and the spike-consistency contribution remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for the weaker membrane-potential variant and hypothesized overfitting of time-resolved alignment, plus an interpretation of the augmentation accuracy/runtime tradeoff. Section 5 newly qualifies deployment claims by identifying backpropagation as a limitation in resource-constrained scenarios. These expand the discussion of mechanisms, operating choices, and applicability.

D1.justification: Appendix D substantially expands documentation with dataset counts, pretrained-model accuracies, Transformer feature dimensions, ConvLSTM layer sizes, a learning-rate search from 0.001 to 0.8, rates fixed across shifted domains, and four RTX 3090 GPUs. These are newly disclosed details, not evidence that retained experiments changed settings. Exact selected learning rates remain unspecified, and code availability is still promised after acceptance.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for AugMix, ImageNet-V2, ImageNet-A, ConvLSTM, and Spike-driven Transformer V3, and removes the LeCun document-recognition reference. The AugMix citation is corrected to the relevant work. The existing related-work discussion and central novelty positioning remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 condenses and rewrites the CNN-results discussion, compresses Algorithm 1 and the equation exposition, reorganizes supplementary sections, and renames the conclusion to include limitations. Most introductory, related-work, and method prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The document switches from two-column to predominantly single-column formatting. Four separate CNN benchmark tables become one transposed table; existing ablation plots are redrawn and combined into Figure 3, with the Gaussian Blur panel removed. New experiments receive additional tables, and the kernel and DVS displays are substantially reformatted.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central empirical case by testing architectural and domain generality beyond CNN corruption benchmarks and directly examining previously untested alignment choices and computational tradeoffs. Added implementation information and an explicit backpropagation limitation improve assessability. A new reporting inconsistency remains: Table 1 gives SPACE's CIFAR-100-C average as 41.58%, although its 15 listed scores average 41.85%. This limited drawback does not outweigh the stronger validation of the paper's principal claims.
